readerTitle: Fourteen numbers on the receipt, one on the whiteboard
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 식료품점, 식단 앱) + 실제 개념 (Lean Analytics의 'One Metric That Matters', 굿하트의 법칙) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 지표를 많이 보는 것이 집중이 아니다. 지금 가장 큰 문제를 보여주는 숫자 하나를 고르면 그 숫자가 모든 아이디어를 거르는 기준이 된다.
misconception: 숫자를 많이 볼수록 사업을 잘 안다. 결국 중요한 숫자는 언제나 매출이다.

sources.text: Croll, A. & Yoshizawa, B. (2013). Lean Analytics. O'Reilly Media. ('One Metric That Matters')
Goodhart, C. (1975), 이후 Strathern, M. (1997)의 표현 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure'
식료품점과 식단 앱 사례, 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 'One Metric That Matters'라는 표현이 Lean Analytics(2013)에 나오는지 출간본으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 책 이름만 언급하고 인용문은 쓰지 않았습니다.
굿하트의 법칙에서 흔히 인용되는 문장은 굿하트 본인이 아니라 Marilyn Strathern(1997)의 요약입니다. 카드에는 인용 없이 원리만 풀어 썼습니다.
가상 수치 확인: 새 손님 10명 중 2명 재방문(20%) → 8주 후 4명(40%). 앱: 가입자 100명 중 15명이 2주차 식단을 만듦(15%). 계산상 문제 없음.

cards.title: Fourteen numbers on the receipt, one on the whiteboard
body: Every night at closing, Mina's register prints a report: sales, transactions, average basket, top items, voids, refunds, hourly traffic and seven more lines.
She reads every line. Six months into running her neighborhood grocery, sales are flat, and she can't say what she changed because of any of them.

image.label: A long register receipt curling off a shop counter
image.brief: 작은 동네 식료품점 계산대. 영수증처럼 긴 일일 리포트가 카운터 아래로 길게 늘어져 있고 숫자가 빼곡함. 뒤쪽 벽에 빈 화이트보드. 따뜻한 저녁 조명. 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: Which number should Mina watch?
body: Her shop gets plenty of first-time visitors from the new apartments nearby. But of every 10 new customers, only about 2 come back within a month.
She has time to really focus on one thing for the next two months. What should she watch?

options.text: All fourteen, a little more carefully each night
options.feedback: She'd stay informed but unfocused. With fourteen signals pulling in different directions, no single idea ever gets a fair test.

options.text: Total weekly sales, because that's what pays the bills
options.feedback: Sales matter, but they're a result of many things at once. Watching them tells her she has a problem, not which lever to pull.

options.text: The share of new customers who return within a month
options.feedback: This points at her biggest problem right now. Every idea can be judged by one question: will it bring people back?

cards.title: One number changed the conversations.
body: Mina wrote "Came back: 2 of 10" on the whiteboard behind the counter and updated it every Monday.

Ideas got easier to sort. A new snack aisle? Maybe later. Asking new customers what they couldn't find, then stocking it? Yes. A staff member started remembering regulars' names. A stamp card rewarded the second visit, not the tenth.
Eight weeks later the board said **4 of 10**. Sales followed.

image.label: Whiteboard behind a counter showing a single number
image.brief: 계산대 뒤 화이트보드에 큰 글씨로 "Came back: 4 of 10". 아래 작은 글씨로 지워진 이전 숫자 "2", "3". 직원 한 명이 손님에게 물건을 건네며 웃는 장면. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Focus on one number
body: **Focusing on one number** means choosing the single measure that best shows your biggest problem right now, making it visible to everyone, and judging each idea by whether it moves that number.
It isn't about ignoring everything else. It's about deciding what wins when ideas compete for your limited time. The book *Lean Analytics* calls this the "one metric that matters" for a given stage.

cards.title: Why one beats fourteen.
body: A small business has little time and few people. One number does several jobs at once.
list: **It settles arguments:** ideas that don't move it wait
**It aligns the team:** everyone knows what a good week looks like
**It speeds learning:** you see within weeks whether a change worked
**It stops busywork:** activity that feels productive but changes nothing becomes obvious
cards.callout: The best number is one you can move, see often, and that reflects real customer behavior.

cards.title: The right number changes as you grow.
body: Early on, the question is often "do people want this enough to come back?" Later it may be "can we reach more of them?" or "does each sale make money?"

A bakery might watch morning sell-out time, then later the cost per loaf. A repair service might watch jobs finished on the first visit. Pick the number for the **problem you have now**, not the one you hope to have.

cards.title: A number you chase can lie to you.
body: Once a measure becomes a target, people find shortcuts. Mina could boost returns with deep second-visit discounts and lose money on each one. Economists call this Goodhart's law.
So keep a few guardrails in the background, like cash and margin, and check they don't fall while your main number rises. And retire the number when its problem is solved.

cards.title: Now it's a meal-planning app.
body: Your small team built an app that plans a week of dinners. Downloads are growing and the app store rating is good. But of every 100 users who sign up, only about 15 create a plan in their second week.
The team tracks a dashboard of twenty charts. Which number goes on the wall?

options.text: Weekly downloads, since growth attracts investors
options.feedback: Downloads are rising already. Pushing them harder fills a leaky bucket faster and hides the real problem.

options.text: Monthly revenue, to prove the business works
options.feedback: Revenue matters eventually, but with few users sticking around it's too small and slow to guide this month's choices.

options.text: Share of new users who make a plan in week two
options.feedback: It targets the biggest gap: people try the app but don't make it a habit. Every feature idea can be tested against it.

cards.title: Find your biggest problem, then give it a number.
body: Many numbers keep you informed. One number keeps you focused, as long as you watch the guardrails and change it when the problem changes.
**Try it today:** write down your business's biggest problem in one sentence. Then write the number that would prove it's getting better, and put it where your team will see it.
